title: Mira's cup of poison
hookLine: a Rajput princess who said she was already married, to Krishna
carry: God can be loved as the beloved
tomorrow: mother, i didn't eat the butter

cards: Rajasthan, in the days of the Rajput kingdoms. The story goes that a little girl in a royal family sees a wedding procession go by and asks her mother: who will I marry?
Her mother, half joking, points to a small image of Krishna and says: him. The girl takes it completely seriously.
She grows up, she's married off to a prince of a powerful royal house, and she tells everyone, calmly, that she was already married. To Krishna. Her name was Mira.
Her songs are still sung today.

teach.h: A PRINCESS OF MERTA AND MEWAR.
teach.b: Tradition remembers Mirabai as a princess of Merta who married into the royal house of Mewar. An honest note first: very little about her is known for certain.
Most of what's told comes from devotional tradition, and many songs sung in her name were likely composed later by others who loved her. But the Mira of those songs and stories is unforgettable.

Her husband, tradition says, died young, and she refused to behave the way a royal widow was expected to. She sang and danced in the temple, in public, with wandering holy people, which scandalized her in-laws.
Her refrain, in a song still widely sung, is roughly: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. Giridhar: the one who lifted the mountain. Gopal: the cowherd.
Her in-laws, tradition says, sent her a cup of poison, disguised as holy water offered to Krishna. Mira drank it, because it came as an offering to her beloved, and it didn't harm her.
Another time, a snake in a basket; when she opened it she found a garland, or an image of Krishna.
Eventually she left the palace for Vrindavan, Krishna's childhood country, and then Dwarka, on the western coast, where tradition says she disappeared into Krishna's image.
What Mira adds to bhakti: the love isn't only reverence. It can be the love of a bride, bold, personal, and willing to lose everything the world thinks matters.

teach.h: GOD CAN BE LOVED AS THE BELOVED.
teach.b: Teachers call it madhurya, the sweet love: God loved as the beloved.

how: Mirabai's bhajans are sung across North India and the diaspora, in temples, homes and concerts; many devotees know her as the model of madhurya bhava, love for Krishna as a beloved.

o: a widow's vow to stay in the palace and keep quiet
a royal duty to marry a prince from a powerful house
love for God as personal as a bride's for her beloved

drunk as an offering, no harm

games.q: you're Mira. your in-laws send you a cup, and say it's holy water offered to Krishna. you suspect it's poison. what does the story say you do?
o: drink it, as an offering to Krishna.
games.why: she drinks it, because it came in Krishna's name. tradition says it did her no harm.

practice: Ask yourself what you'd keep if everything else were taken: not things, but the love you'd walk out of a palace for, a person, a faith, maybe something you've never said aloud. Let it stand plainly, without apology.
If you pray, hold it up to God as Mira held up hers; if not, just let it be yours.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti yoga, through Mirabai: the Rajput poet-saint whose love for Krishna was the love of a bride, bold and personal. Mine is Giridhar Gopal.

orig.note: Hindi/Braj: Giridhar Gopal, 'the mountain-lifter, the cowherd,' Mira's name for Krishna.

carryVoice: Your line: God can be loved as the beloved. Some loves are worth walking out of a palace for. That's day two seventy-one.
